"  I  am  not  able  to  resist  the  temptation  of  congratalating  you

General  Congress  of  Columbia,  and  published  throughout  the  Re- 
public.   On  an  amendment  proposed,  that  the  period  of  emancipa- 
tion should  be  fixed  at  the  age  of  twenty-five  years  instead  of 
eighteen,  there  were  ten  votes  to  one  against  the  amendment.  Such 
was  the  horror  with  which  slavery  was  viewed  by  that  assembly, 
composed  of  the  most  enlightened  men  from  every  district,  and  many 
of  them  considerable  Slave-holders !  Others,  who  have  large  estates 
cultivated  by  free  labourers,  were  the  foremost  to  support  the  pro- 
perty tax,  for  purchasing  the  freedom  of  those  not  entitled  to  it  by 
military  service,  born  previous  to  the  publication  of  the  law.  What 
has  been  the  consequence  ?    The  Slaves  are  all  peaceably  at  work 
throughout  the  Republic,  as  well  as  the  newly  enfranchised  and 
those  originally  free.    But  the  watch-word  of  oppression  is,  that 
certain  nations  and  classes  are  not  sufllcieutly  enlightened  to  be 
free ;  and  for  this  reason  these  interested  politicians  would  willingly 
perpetuate  their  slavery  and  ignorance  to  the  latest  period  of  time. 
If  it  were  necessary  to 'freedom  that  every  man  should  legislate  in 
hb  own  person,  thjs  argument  would  have  some  weight.    Other- 
wise, from  parity  of  reasoning,  a  certain  proportion  of  the  peasantry 
in  Great  BriUin  and  Ireland  had  better  be  slaves.    Wlthdat  going 
further,  I  am  fully  convinced  that  the  prosperity,  secnrity,  and 
general  happiness  of  Columbia  have  been  best  consulted  by  this 
law,  and  the  morality  of  the  people  essentially  prmnoted.

interest  vhich  this  House  has  so  long  taken,  and  still 
continues  to  take,  in  the  Abolition  of  the  Slave  Trade, 
has  led  as  to  peruse  with  no  little  solicitude  the  papers 
relative  to  that  subject,  which,  by  his  Majesty's  com- 
mands, were  lately  laid  before  us  : — and  that  we  could 
not  forbear  indulging  a  hope  that  his  Majesty's  renewed 
representations  and  remonstrances  would  have  at  length 
produced  the  desired  effect  of  causing  the  various  Go- 
vernments, by  whose  subjects  the  Slave  Trade  was 
still  carried  on,  seriously  to  consider  the  numerous 
and  powerful  obligations  under  which  they  lay,  to  co- 
operate with  his  Majesty,  heartily  and  efficiently,  in 
order  to  put  an  end  for  ever  to  this  enormous  evil : 

"  But  that  we  have  learned  with  grief  and  shame, 
that,  with  very  few  exceptions,  every  hope  of  this 
nature  has  been  altogether  frustrated  ;  and  that  we  are 
still  compelled  to  witness  the  strange  and  humiliating 

e 


I 

spectacle^  of  practices  which  are  acknowledged  to  be 
made  up  of  wickedness  and  craelty,  by  the  very  Go- 
vernments whose  subjects  are  nevertheless  carrying 
them  on  upon  a  great  and  continually  augmented  scale: 

**  That  we  observe,  however,  with  satisfaction,  that 
the  powerful  reasoning  and  continued  expostulations 
of  his  Majesty's  Government,  enforced  by  the  strong 
and  persevering  remonstrances  of  his  Mcyesty's  Am- 
bassador at  the  Court  of  the  Netherlands,  have  at  length 
produced  an  admission  of  the  just  construction  of  the 
treaty  with  that  power : 

''  That  we  are  glad  also  to  see  that  some  of  the  abuses 
have  been  corrected,  which  had  prevailed  in  the  con- 
duct of  the  courts  of  mixed  jurisdiction  at  Sierra  Leone ; 
but  that  experience  has  proved  the  necessity  of  altering 
that  provision  which  renders  it  necessary  for  the  Slaves 
to  have  been  actually  on  ship-board  to  justify  the  con- 
demnation of  the  vessel,  and  of  allowing  due  weight  to 
be  given  to  that  decisive  proof  of  the  object  of  the 
voyage,  which  is  afforded  by  the  peculiar  mode  of  fitting 
and  equipping  Slave-ships : 

'^  That  it  is  some  alleviation  of  the  pain  produced 
by  the  almost  uniform  tenor  of  these  distressing  ac- 
counts, to  learn,  that  the  Cortes  of  Spain  has  subjected 
all  who  should  be  found  concerned  in  Slave-trading  to 
a  severe  and  infamous  punishment :  and  that,  with  this 
evidence  of  a  just  estimate  of  the  guilt  of  the  crime, 
we  cannot  but  hope  that  they  will  not  rest  satisfied  with 
a  legal  prohibition,  but  that  they  will  provide  the  requi- 
site means  for  carrying  their  law  into  execution: 

"  That  we  find  with  concern,  that  the  vessels  of  Por- 
tugal, so  far  from  retiring  gradually  from  the  trade,  have 
been  carrying  it  on  with  increased  activity,  more  espe- 
cially on  that  very  part  of  the  coast  which  is  to  the  north 


li 

of  the  Lino,  in  direct  violation  of  the  treaty  by  which  she 
had  stipolated  to  confine  her  trade  to  the  sonth  of  it : 

'^  That  we  cannot  but  cherish  the  hope,  that  the 
new  Government  of  Portugal  will  manifest  a  warmer 
zeal  for  enforcing  a  treaty  which  every  law,  divine  and 
human,  binds  her  to  observe: 

**  That  we  have  observed  with  no  little  pleasure  the 
zeal  for  the  Abolition  of  the  Slave  Trade  that  has  been 
manifested  by  the  commanders  of  the  ships  of  war  of 
the  United  States  of  America  employed  on  the  coast  of 
Africa,  and  the  disposition  they  have  shewn  to  co-ope<^ 
rate  with  the  officers  of  his  Majesty's  Navy  for  their 
common  object;  but  that  we  are  concerned  to  have 
perceived  in  the  American  Government  no  disposition 
to  give  up  the  objections  it  formerly  urged  against 
the  establishment  of  a  mutual  right  of  examining  each 
other's  ships  on  the  coast  of  Africa  : 

"  That  we  had  hoped  that  the  powerful  arguments 
urged  by  a  Committee  of  the  House  of  Representa- 
tives, in  favour  of  this  arrangement,  would  have  their 
just  weight,  more  especially  that  which  points  out  the 
difiTerence,  or  rather  contrariety,  between  this  conven* 
tional  and  qualified  system,  and  the  right  of  searching 
neutral  vessels  without  any  previous  treaty,  as  claimed 
and  practised  in  war ;  above  all,  that  the  consideration 
so  strongly  enforced,  that  it  is  only  by  the  general  esta- 
blishment  of  some  such  system  that  the  trade  can  ever 
be  effectually  abolished,  would  have  induced  the  Ame- 
rican  Government  to  consent  to  it,  when  the  object  in 
question  involves  the  rights  and  happiness  of  so  large  a 
portion  of  our  fellow-creatures. 

*'  That  with  the  deepest  concern  we  find,  as  in  the 
last  year,  vessels  under  the  French  flag  trading  for  Slaves 
along  the  whole  extent  of  the  coast  of  Africa :— That  at

Ill 

home  and  abroad  proposals  are  circnlated  for  Slave-trad- 
ing voyages,  inviting  the  smallest  capitals,  and  tempting 
adventurers  by  the  hopes  of  enormoas  profits : — That  the 
few  ships  of  war  of  that  country  stationed  in  Africa 
offer  no  material  obstruction  to  the  trade,  nor  do  the 
Governors  of  her  colonies  appear  to  •  be  more  active ; 
and  all  this,  while  the  French  Government  reprobates 
the  traffic  in  the  strongest  termSi  and  declares  that  it  is 
using  its  utmost  efforts  for  the  prevention  of  so  great  an 
evil : — That  it  is  deeply  to  be  regretted  that  a  Govern- 
ment which  has  been  generally  regarded  as  eminent  for 
its  efficiency,  should  here  alone  find  its  efforts  so  entirely 
paralized  :-Tbat  meanwhile  we  can  only  continue  to 
lament  that  a  great  and  gallant  nation,  eminently  fa- 
voured by  Providence  with  natural  advantages,  and 
among  the  very  foremost  in  all  the  distinctions  and  en- 
joyments of  civilized  life,  should  thus,  on  its  restoration 
to  the  blessings  of  peace,  and  to  the  government  of  its 
legitimate  sovereign,  appear  in  fact  to  be  the  chief 
agent  in  blasting  the  opening  prospects  of  civilization 
which  even  Africa  had  begun  to  present,  and  in  pro- 
longing the  misery  and  barbarism  of  that  vast  continent: 

"  That,  on  the  whole,  we  coqjure  his  Majesty  to  renew 
his  remonstrances,  and  to  render  it  manifest  that  his 
interference  has  not  been  a  matter  of  form,  but  of  se- 
rious and  urgent  duty : 

**  That  this  country  will  at  least  have  the  satisfaction 
of  knowing  that  we  have  been  active  and  unwearied  in 
making  reparation  to  Africa*  for  the  wrongs  with  which 
we  ourselves  were  so  long  chargeable ;  and  we  cannot 
doubt  that  we  s^all  ultimately  be  able  to  congratulate 
his  Majesty  on  the  success  of  his  endeavours,  and  on 
his  having  had  a  principal  share  in  wiping  away  the 
foulest  blot  on  the  character  of  Christendom/'

there  is  no  reason  for  despondency  concerning  the

tution to  promote,  the  final  and  entire  Abolition 
of  the  Slave  Trade ;  so,  on  the  other,  there  is 
a  loud  and  urgent  call  on  all  the  friends  of  that; 
measure  for  renewed  and  increased  exertions.  , 
..  The  grand  instrument  on  which,  under  the  bless- 
ing  of  Providence,  they  must  rely,  for  the  accom- 
plishment of  their  purpose,  is  public  opinion.      .  , 

In  this  country,  few  persons  of  common  inforr 
mation  are  ignorant  of  the  nature  and  effects  of 
the  Slave  Trade;  but  in  foreign  countries  the 
case  is  very  different.  There,  many,  who  may  be 
termed  well-informed  people,  are  under  the  great- 
est misconception  on  those  points;  and  hence 
they  become  the  dupes  of  those,  among  us  ex« 
ploded,  falsehoods  by  which  this  cruel  traffic  was 
so  long  excused  and  even  justified.

lating  publications  of  various  sorts  throughout  thQ 
Continent  of  Europe,  to  sweep  away  these  wretched 
fallacies,  and  to  describe  the  trade  in  its  true  char

by  the  vigilance  of  British  cmizers  from  finding  any  shelter

18  due  to  the  general  obligations  of  justice  and  humanity :

That  since  we  are  now  aware  of  its  real  character,  it  becomes

the  truth  on  others  who  may  have  been  misled  by  our  ex- 
ample :  and  as  we  contributed  so  largely  to  prolong  the 
misery  and  barbarism  of  the  Africans,  we  should  now  be 
proportionably  earnest  in  using  the  means  with  which  Provi- 
dence has  endowed  us,  for  promoting  their  civilization  and 
happiness.

.  '*  Having  concluded  my  remarks  on  the  island  of  Fernando 
I^Oy  and  the  several  settlements  in  Africa,  visited  during  the

currence whatever. 

<<  Witoessing,  as  I  have  for  the  last  three  years,  the  Slave 
Trade  in  all  its  horrors,  it  would  give  me  the  siocerest  satis- 
&ction  if  I  could  with  truth  report  that  it  was  really  de- 
clining ;  but  if  I  did  so,  I  should  only  mblead  their  lordriiips,

servation justify  my  saying,  that,  in  the  manner  of  conducting 
it,  in  cruelty  and  brutality  it  canjiot  be  surpassed.

**  The  Slave  Trade  at  Whydah  is  conducted  to  a  very 
great  extent  by  a  Portuguese  renegado,  named  de  Souza, 
whp»  banbhed  from  the  Brasib,  has  fixed  himself  at  Whydah, 
where  he  is  the  agent  or  Slave-factor  to  the  Brazilian  Nation, 
and  lives  in  prodigious  splendour ;  assumes  the  rights  and 
privileges  of  a  person  in  authority,  granting  papers  and 
licences  to  the  Slave-traders  in  all  the  form  and  confidence 
of  one  empowered  to  do  so  by  the  Portuguese  Government. 
The  extent  of  the  Slave  Trade  at  Whydah  may  be  judged 
of  by  the  number  of  Portuguese  vessels  anchoring  off  this  port 
and  Lagos  annually,  being  generally  calculated  at  100,  and 
for  no  other  purpose  than  to  obtain  Shves*  These  vessels, 
if  met  at  sea  and  boarded  by  a  British  cruizer,  report  them- 
selves bound  to  Cabenda  and  Molemba ;  and,  if  they  have 
left  the  coast  of  Benin  a  day  only,  they  declare  themselves 
to  have  sailed  from  the  above-mentioned  ports,  or  even  from 
the  more  southern  parts  of  the  coast  of  Aagohu  Thus,  though 
a  vessel  receiving  a  cargo  of  Slaves  at  Whydah  is  subject  to 
capture  provided  she  be  met  with  before  she  pass  the  limits 
of  aeisure,  she  avoids  this  by  her  short  run,  until  she  is  in 
security  by  passing  south  of  the  Line;  and  then,  if  met  with 
and  boarded^  the  master  has  a  ready  answer.  The  ship's 
log,  if  fairly  kept,  will  be  at  variance  with  his  declaration ;

We  have  not  been  able  to  obtain  a  Copy  of  the  Report;  but 
we  understand  that  it  is  founded  generally  upon  the  hospi- 
tality due  to  the  vessel  of  a  friendly  nation,  driven  into  these 
seas  by  stress  of  weather,  and  not  in  a  condition  to  pursue 
her  voyage. 

**  In  the  confidential  conversations  which  have  subse* 
quentty  passed  upon  this  subject,  we  have  not  been  able  to 
obtain  any  more  satisfactory  explanation  of  the  transaction ; 
and  although  the  grounds  upon  which  the  legal  counsel  are 
said  to  have  rested  their  Report, — namely,  the  arrival  at  thb 
port,  through  stress  of  weather,  of  a  Portuguese  vessel,  with 
Negroes  on  board, — ^are  highly  improbable,  not  to  say  impos- 
sible, and  moreover  do  not  by  any  means  authorise  the 
violation  of  our  treaty,  and  of  his  Catholic  Majesty's  decree ; 
yet,  upon  mature  deliberation,  we  were  clearlyof  opinion  that 
we  are  not  warranted  by  your  lordship's  instructions  to  make 
any  official  representation  or  remonstrance  upon  the  case.''

*•  LAW  OF  MANOMISSION  OP  SLAVES. 

^  The  General  Congress  of  Columbia  considering,-^ 

"  1st,  That  the  last  Congress  of  Vanezuela  very  urgently 
recommended  to  that  of  Columbia  to  take  into  their  con - 
oideration  the  situation  of  the  Slaves  that  existed  in  the  ter- 
sitory  of  the  Republic  : 

"  2d,  That,  according  to  the  eternal  principles  of  reason, 

justice,  and  the  wisest  policy,  no  Republican  Government,  truly 

just  and  philanthropic,  can  exist  without  seeking  to  alleviate 

all  those  classes  of  mankind  that  are  degraded  and  unhappy : 

'^  8d,  and  lastly.  That  an  object  of  such  importance  to  the 
Republic  ought  to  be  realised,  and  slavery  be  gradually 
abolished  ;  so  that,  without  compromising  the  public  tran- 
quillity, or  affecting  the  rights  which  the  proprietors  really 
possess,  the  freedom  of  all  the  inhabitants  of  Colombia  may 
in  a  few  years  be  ensured : 

**  Have  decreed  as  follows. — 

"  Article  I.  The  children  of  Slaves  bora  from  the  day  of 
publication  of  this  Law  in  the  capitals  of  the  provinces  sliall 
be  free ;  and,  as  such,  their  names  shall  be  inserted  in  the 
municipal  and  parish  registries. 

"  II.  The  owners  of  the  mothers  shall  be  bound  to  bring  «p^ 
clothe,  and  nourish  their  children  that  are  bora  from  the  day 
of  publication  of  this  Order;  but  these  shall,  as  recompense, 
indemnify  the  owners  of  their  mothers  the  expenses  incurred 
in  the  rearing  tbem  by  their  labour  and  service,  which  (ky

was  collected  when  it  rained.  It  appears  they  had  met 
vtry  baffling  winds  and  calms.  The  day  on  which  the  sad 
disaster  occurred  was  rainy,  with  frequent  tornados  and 
very  little  wind  :  they  had  set  their  foresail,  mainsail,  and 
two  jibs :  a  whirlwind  suddenly  came  on,  and  in  an  instant 
of  time  upset  the  vessel,  which,  melaocholy  to  relate,  sunk 
with  the  whole  of  the  Slaves  and  six  of  the  crew.  The  rest 
of  the  crew  (eleven)  succeeded  in  saving  the  small  boat ; 
and,  as  already  stated,  were  nine  days  in  it  before  they  ^ 
reached  Cape  Mount.  Their  privations  and  sufferings 
were  so  great,  that  several  of  them  have  since  died."

way  to  the  Havaunah  market ;  for  it  is  rather  incredible, 
that  so  many  Slaves  could  be  required  in  their  West-India 
possessions.  Numerical  calculations  we  will  not  now  enter 
into :  in  fact,  if  at  all  correct,  they  must  from  their  magni- 
tude appear  incredible. 

"  The  increase  of  this  horrid  traffic  is  sensibly  felt  in  this 
colony;  and  indeed  it  is  truly  painful  to  reflect  that  the 
exertions  of  our  Government,  in  effecting  its  total  abolition, 
should  be  thwarted  by  the  torpidity  and  indifference  of  those 
powers  whose  good  faith  stands  pledged,  by  their  public 
declarations,  for  its  suppression.  At  no  very  remote  period, 
the  traffickers  in  human  blood,  however  numerous  on  the 
coast,  could  not  with  impunity  visit  the  rivers  in  our  vici- 
nity; but  now,  with  unparalleled  audacity,  they  anchor 
almost  within  view  of  the  British  flag.  Even  at  the  moment 
we  now  write,  a  French  vessel  is  taking  in  her  Slaves  at 
Shebar,  a  few  miles  south  of  the  Bananas ;  and  a  Spaniard, 
the  Rosalia,  Don  Francisco  Freyre  master,  waiting  for  a 
similar  cargo,  not  forty  miles  from  the  Isles  de  Los !"

'^  In  a  former  Namber,  we  adverted  to  the  circumstanoe

"  The  schooner  — — ,  Don  Morales  master,  arrived 
in  the  Rio  Pongos  during  the  month  of  August  last,  where 
she  took  on  board  200  Slaves,  and  sailed  in  the  beginning  of

the  master  (Morales),  when  trading  for  his  cargo,  exhibited 
many  instances  of  a  ferocity  of  character  towards  his  Slaves ; 
but  it  appears  that  after  leaving  the  river  his  cruelty  had  its 
full  scope.  The  number  of  Slaves  on  board  being  quite 
disproportionate  to  the  stowage  of  the  schooner,  he  was 
obliged  from  the  first  to  issue  short  rations  of  water  and 
rice,  in  consequence  of  which  some  discontent  was  manifest, 
ed  by  the  Slaves.  Morales,  deaf  to  their  wants,  by  way  of 
punishment,  kept  them  all  below  for  three  days  without  food 
of  any  kind ;  and,  with  a  barbarity  unparalleled,  except 
amongst  Slave-dealers,  discharged  all  the  fire-arms  in  his 
vessel  into  the  hold  upon  the  poor  victims,  bound  down  and 
fastened  to  each  other  with  chains.  Some  of  the  sailors 
presumed  to  interfere;  but  thb  barbarian  silenced  their 
clamour,  by  cutting  off  the  head  of  the  most  forward  with  hb 
sabre.  He  then  made  sail  again  for  the  Rio  Pongos,  where, 
with  the  assistance  of  the  Slave-fiictors,  he  got  every  thing 
put  to  rights,  took  in  Slaves  to  supply  the  number  killed* 
and  again  sailed  for  the  Havannah.

Sir — Permit  me  to  have  recourse  to  your  journal,  in  order 
to  express  my  regret  that  a  periodical  work,  which  1  devote 
exclusively  to  science,  and  more  particularly  to  the  studies 
connected  with  my  art,  should  have  served  as  a  text  for  se- 
lions  reproaches  on  the  French  Government,  delivered  yes- 
terday. In  the  Chamber  of  Deputies,  by  an  honourable  mem- 
ber, who  perhaps  gave  way  with  too  much  vehemence  to  a 
generous  emotion  of  philanthropy. 

I  allude  to  a  statement  inserted  in  one  of  the  Numbers  of 
the  BibHothique  Opktalmologique,  dated  the  30th  of  Novem- 
ber, 1810.  I  there  gave  an  account  of  a  contagious  ophthal* 
mia  which  occurred  among  the  crew  of  a  Slave-ship,  and 
the  details  of  which  were  furnished  to  me  by  the  captain, 
surgeon,  and  several  of  the  seamen,  who  came  to  Paris  ta^ 
entrust  themselves  to  my  care. 

In  that  account,  I  stated  the  names  ofthe  ship  and  of  the 
captain ;  but  having  learned  that  a  provincial  journal  had 
seized  upon  the  facts,  and  misrepresented  them,  I  hastened 
to  recal  the  Number  which  contained  the  account,  only  a 
i^w  copies  of  which  had  been  distributed,  and  to  cause  it  to 
be  reprinted  with  the  names  suppressed,  and  the  facts  re- 
stated in  a  shape  more  conformable  to  the  spirit  of  my  work, 
which  is  devoted  entirely  to  medical  science. 

I  feel,  Mr.  Editor,  that  I  owe  to  the  public  this  profes- 
sion of  principles.  Those  who  know  me  are  aware  that  I 
htive  nothing  so  mnch  at  heart  as  the  tranquillity  of  my

S16  APPENDIX  Q. 

capitab  were  embarked  in  the  Slave  Trade  ;  ricli  cities  were 
proud  of  beiog  indebted  to  it  for  their  wealth  and  grandeur  i 
the  sea  was  covered  with  their  ships;  the  abominable  acts 
of  cruelty,  which  ever  attend  the  efforts  to  procure  the 
Negroes  on  the  coast  of  Africa,  and  their  conveyance  to  the 
West  Indies^  were  shrouded  by  a  thick  veil.  Those  only 
whom  avarice  had  attracted  on  board  Slave-ships  knew  the 
dreadful  secrets ;  and  men's  minds  were  every  wher«  deeply 
imbued  with  the  prejudice,  that  the  fate  of  the  principal 
European  States  depended  on  the  prosperity  of  their  colonies^ 
and  that  the  maintenance  of  that  prosperity  depended  on  the 
rapid  increase  of  the  Slave  Trade,  and  the  continual  aug- 
mentation of  a  Slave-population,  which  it  was  impossible  to 
recruit  by  any  other  means. 

"  Such  was  the  state  of  things  in  1785 ;  such  the  obstacles 
which  were  then  to  be  surmounted. 

**  Those  whom  duty  now  calls  to  plead  the  cause  of  the 
Africans,  are  placed  in  far  more  favourable  circumstances. 
Their  task  appears  comparatively  smooth  and  easy.  Thanks 
to  the  efforts  of  their  precursors,  the  work  of  religion  and 
humanity  is  almost  accomplished.  The  Slave  Trade  is  no 
longer  defended  either  on  the  score  of  law  or  principle. 
The  horrors  which  ever  march  in  its  train  have  been  unfold- 
ed at  the  bar  of  the  English  Parliament,  and  demonstrated 
with  an  irresistible  force  of  evidence.  In  point  of  fact,  it  is 
now  abolished.  All  the  nations  of  the  civilized  world  arc 
agreed  on  this  point ;  and  their  sovereigns,  assembled  at  the 
Congress  of  Vienna,  have,  by  an  authentic  and  solemn  act, 
consigned  this  scourge  of  Africa  to  the  execration  of  man- 
kind. The  experience  of  fifteen  years  has  justified  the  pre- 
dictions of  men  versed  in  political  economy,  and  proved  that 
the  colonies  may  prosper  without  the  aid  of  a  constantly 
renewed  and  increasing  importation  of  Slaves.  Those  mer- 
chants who,  urged  by  motives  of  disgraceful  cupidity,  now 
endeavour  to  revive  or  perpetuate  this  horrible  traihc,  have 
really  no  excuse.  They  prove  themselves  rebels  to  the  laws 
of  the  country,  and  deaf  to  the  voice  of  conscience :  they 
deserve  neither  consideration,  nor  lenity,  nor  pity.

on  this  point  corresponds  with  the  law  of  the  15th  of  April, 
1818,  inflicts  on  those  who  embark  in  the  Slave  Trade, — first, 
the  confiscation  of  the  ship  and  cargo,  a  penalty  that  ex- 
tends to  all  the  parties  concerned;  secondly,  the  prohibi- 
tion to  navigate,  a  punishment  which  fails  only  on  the  cap- 
tfun  of  the  ship. 

"  With  regard  to  the  first  of  these  penalties,  there  is  a* 
observation  that  must  immediately  strike  every  man  accus- 
tomed to  consider  such  subjects.  To  lose  his  ship  and  caigo 
is  a  risk  to  which  every  one  who  speculates  in  maritime  trade 
is  exposed.  This  risk  is  more  or  less  serious,  more  or  less 
menacing,  according  to  the  nature  of  the  cargo,  the  good- 
ness of  the  ship,  the  length  of  the  voyage,  the  season  at 
which  it  is  undertaken,  and  the  seas  that  are  to  be  navigated. 
This  risk  may  be  pretty  accurately  estimated,  and  reduced 
to  figures ;  and  it  then  only  remains  to  compare  the  chances

mS  )tom  with  Ibe  cbancct  of  profit  If  the  former  predomi- 
■atc  over  tbe  latter,  the  speculation  is  abandoned :  in  tbe 
contrary  case,  it  is  pursued  in  spite  of  the  risk. 

''  Now,  what  has  been  done  by  the  law  of  the  16tfi  of 
April,  1818?  It  adds  a  new  chance  of  loss  to  the  chances 
which,  in  the  very  nature  of  things,  are  already  incurred  by 
the  merchants  who  carry  on  the  SkiTe  Trade :  it  imposes  a 
new  risk  on  the  traffic.  This  being  done,  if  the  new  risk  be 
such  as  to  predominate  over  the  chances  of  profit,  the  Slave 
Trade  will  cease :  in  the  contrary  case,  it  will  be  carried  on 
without  difficulty* 

'*  Now,  what  is  this  risk?  It  is,  in  the  first  place,  that 
of  being  captured  by  a  small  squadron  of  ships  cruismg 
aloBg  a  coast  of  only  forty  leagues  in  front  of  our  African 
establishments,  while  the  trade  may  be  earned  on  along  an 
immense  extent  of  coast.  It  is,  moreover,  the  danger  of 
being  caught  in  the  very  act  of  landing  Slaves  in  our  co- 
lonies :  for  it  may  be  seen,  on  examining  the  papen.  of 
Is  iSbicc^,  that  the  public  functionaries  are  not  aathoriscd  to 
seise  Negroes  when  they  are  once  landed,  and  have  passed 
what  are  termed  let  Pas  Geomehiqius;  that  is  to  say,  about 
fifty  toises  from  the  shore. 

**  I  have  just  observed  that  this  risk  is  capable  of  being 
valued.  And,  in  point  of  fact,  as  every  one  knows,  maritime 
risks  are  not  in  general  incurred  by  the  owners  of  ships;  but 
for  ages  past,  they  have  been  the  subject  of  a  particular 
contract,  called  a  Policy  of  Insurance, — by  means  of  which, 
tbe  hasards  of  the  adventure  are  transferred,  on  the  payment 
of  a  premium,  more  or  less  considerable,  to  companies  who 
guarantee  to  the  owners  the  restitution  of  their  capital  iq 
case  of  loss. 

**  This  being  the  ease,  the  only  effect  which  the  law  can 
have  is  to  augment  the  premium  of  insurance,  paid  by 
Skive  dealers,  and  consequently  to  reduce  their  profits  in 
that  proportion.  And  if  the  premium  be  not  so  high  as  to 
absorb  the  profits,  or  if  it  do  not  reduce  them  below  their 
ordinary  rate,  it  is  certab  that  the  law  must  be  inefficient, 
and  that  the  trada  will  proceed  without  obstruction.

▼incing  evidence  that  these  demands  had  the  fatal  effect  of

It  has  been  proved,  on  the  best  authority,  that  famine,  devas- 
tation, and  continual  warfare  undertaken  for  the  sole  pur- 
pose of  procuring  prisoners,  were  the  inevitable  consequences

golation,  but  furnished  the  arms,  nouiished  the  hatred,  and 
fomented  the  discord  which  produced  it.

'' '  Never,'  said  Mr.  Wilberforce,  in  the  EoglUh  Parlia-

Uepid :  violence  is  in  general  exempt  from  perfidy,  and  daring 
iniquity  from  meanness.  But  there  is  no  benign  concomitant 
here :  it  belongs  to  this*  hateful  traffic  to  deteriorate  alike  the 
good  and  the  bad,  and  even  to  pollute  crime  itself:  it  is  a  state 
of  warfare  undignified  by  courage :  it  is  a  state  of  peace  in 
which  there  is  no  security  against  devastation  and  massacre. 
There  you  find  the  vices  of  polished  society,  without  the 
delicacy  of  manners  by  which  they  are  tempered ;  the  ,pri-

**  What  can  I  add.  Gentlemen,  to  these  admirable  senti- 
ments?    Certainly  nothing;  and  yet  the  great  and  good

Neither  the  long  existence  of  the  traffic,  nor  its  destructive 
effects,   have  proved  useless  to   the  cause  of  humanity. 
Providence  has  suffered  both  to  exist  for  our  instruction ;  to 
make  known  to  us  the  dreadful  facility  with  which  civilized 
man  may  resume  the  ferocity  of  the  savage ;  to  exhibit  to  us 
also  the  omnipotence  of  justice,  virtue,  and  couragepus  per-

example,   how  petty  and  contemptible,  how  feeble  and 
worthless,  are  the  most  firmly  established  interests,  and  the 
most  inveterate  prejudices,  when  opposed  to  truth.     Forty 
years  have  not  yet  passed  away  since  a  young  clergyman, 
unknown,  friendless,  and  without  fortune,  first  denounced 
the  Slave  Trade,  in  a  Latin  Dissertation  addressed  to  the 
University  of  Cambridge.     Within  seven  years  from  that 
time  all  the  talent  in  Europe  was  leagued  in  the  cause ;  and 
fifteen  years  have  already  elapsed  since  it  triumphed  both 
in  the  old  and  the  new  world.     Those  who  concurred  in 
achieving  this  glorious  work  are  now  numbered  among  the 
benefactors  of  mankind.    Their  memory  will  never  die,  but 
their  work  may  perish.    It  is  in  our  power,  it  is  in  the 
power  of  onr  criminal  negligence,  to  deprive  a  Granville 
Sharpe,  a  Clarkson,  and  a  Wilberforce,  of  the  fruit  of  their 
labours  and  their  watchings.     Is  it  in   this  way  that  we 
would  wish  to  associate  ourselves  with  their  renown  ?    Shall 
we  consent  to  load  ourselves  with  this  ignominy  in  the  eyes 
of  posterity— we  who,  during  the  lives  of  those  distinguished 
men,  have  already  treasured  up  their  names  to  transmit  them 
to  the  admiration  and  gratitude  of  the  remotest  generations?

''  Art.  II.— The  Committee  will  collect  all  kinds  of  informa-

**  The  Slave  Trade  has  been  checked  by  our  cruisers  upon 
the  southern  coasts  of  the  United  States ;  and  no  great  at- 
tempts appear  to  have  been  made  to  introduce  Slaves  through 
illicit  channels.

Savannah :  forty  or  fifty  more  have  been  sent  out  of  that  State, 
under  what  orders  it  is  not  known.

^  The  Slave  Trade  is  carried  on  briskly  in  this  neighbour- 
hood. Had  I  authority  so  to  do,  I  could  take  a  vessel 
lying  within  the  floating  of  one  tide,  say  twenty-five  miles 
ftom  us,  in  tfie  Sbebar,  under  American  cotours,  takmg  in  a 
cargo  of  Slaves.  Their  policy  is  to  come  with  a  cargo  of 
goods  suited  to  the  market,  deliver  it  to  a  Slave-factor  on 
shore,  and  contract  for  Slaves.  They  then  lie  at  anchor  in 
the  river,  or  stand  out  to  sea  for  a  specified  number  of  days, 
till  the  Slaves  are  all  procured  and  brought  to  the  beach, 
and  placed  under  a  hovel  or  shed  prepared  for  the  purpose, 
all  chained  two  and  two.  At  the  appointed  time,  or  on  a 
concerted  signal,  the  vessel  comes  in  and  takes  her  Slaves  on 
board,  and  is  off  in  an  hour.  This  is  rendered  necessary,  as 
they  cannot  be  seized  unless  they  have  Slaves  on  board  ;  and 
they  are  watched  by  the  cruisers,  so  as  to  be  taken  when 
they  have  Slaves  with  them.  The  Augusta  (the  schooner  I 
purchased)  is  a  vessel  of  104  tons,  a  swift  sailor,  and  was 
intended  to  take  a  cargo  of  100.  She  had  a  caboose 
fitted  to  boil  rice  in  laiige  quantities  :  Slaves  receive  one  pint 
each  per  day/'

**  The  inkmoral  and  pernicious  practice  of  the  SlaV^^Trade, 
has  attnctcd  much  public  attention  io  Europe  within  the  hat 
four  yeara ;  wA  n  a  Congreaa  at  Vienna,  on  the  0th  of  Feb* 
maiy,  1815,  five  of  the  principal  Powers  made  a  aolemii 
engagement,  in  the  fiice  of  mankind,  that  this  traffic  should 
be  made  to  cease;  in  pursuance  of  which,  these  Powers 
have  enacted  municipal  laws  to  suppress  the  trade.  Spain^ 
though  not  a  party  lo  the  original  engag;ement,  did  aooil 
ailer,  in  her  treaty  with  England,  stipulate  for  the  immediate 
Abolition  of  the  Spanish  Slave-trade  to  the  north  of  the 
Equator,  and  fbr  its  final  and  universal  abolition  on  ihe  30th 
of  May,  1820.  Portugal  likewise,  in  her  treaty  in  1817» 
stipulated  that  the  Portuguese  Skve-trade  on  the  coast  of 
Africa  should  entirely  cease,  to  the  north  of  the  Equator; 
and  engaged  that  it  should  be  unlawful  for  her  subjects  to 
purchase  or  trade  in  Slaves,  except  to  the  southward  of  the 
Line.  The  precise  period  at  which  the  entire  Abolition  is  to 
take  pkce  in  Portugal,  does  not  appear  to  be  finally  fixed : 
but  the  Portuguese  ambassador,  in  the  presence  of  the  Con- 
gress at  Vienna,  declared  that  Portugal,  faithful  to  her  prin- 
ciples, would  not  refuse  to  adopt  the  term  of  eight  years ; 
which  term  will  expire  in  the  year  1823. 

'^  At  this  time,  among  the  EuropeuQ  Stiites,  there  is  not  a 
flag  which  can  legally  cover  this  inhuman  traffic  to  the  north 
of  the  Line.  Nevertheless,  experience  has  proved  the  in- 
efficacy  of  the  various  and  rigorous  laws  which  have  been 
made  in  Europe  and  in  this  country ;  it  being  a  lamentable 
ftct,  that  the  disgraceful  practice  is  now  carried  on  to  a  sur- 
prizing extent  During  the  last  year.  Captain  Trenchard^ 
the  commander  of  the  United  States'  sloop  of  war  the  Cyane^, 
fimnd  that  part  of  the  coast  of  Africa  which  he  visited  lined 
with  vessels,  engaged,  as  it  Is  presumed,  in  this  forbidden . 
traffic.  Of  these  he  examined  many ;  and  five,  which  appeared 
to  be  fitt^  out  on  American  account,  he  sent  into  the  juris- 
diction of  the  United  States  for  adjudication  :  each  of  them,; 
it  is  bdieved,  his  beeil  condemned,  and  the -commanders  of 
two  of  them  have  been  sentenced  to  the  punishment  pre- 
scribed by  the  kws  of  the  United  States.

**  Dariag  our  stay  at  Steifa  Leone,  the  European  gentle- 
men who  were  residents  at  the  place  treated  us  with  the 
utmost  respect,  striving  who  ihould  be  most  forward  in  at- 
tention and  hospitality.  A  party  was  formed  by  those  gen- 
tlemen to  shew  our  officers  the  interior  settlements;  and 
firom  their  report  on  their  return,  I  learned  the  extent  of  the 
colony,  and  die  benevolent  philanthropy  of  the  British  na- 
tion in  alleviating  the  miseries  of  the  oppressed  and  ignorant 
Africans.  Not  less  than  6000  captured'  Africans  have  been 
landed  at  tins  settlement  by  the  British  ships  of  war.  On 
their  arrival,  those  of  a  proper  age  are  named  and  sent  to 
the  adjacent  villages.  A  house  and  lot  is  appointed  to  each 
family ;  and  they  are  supported  one  year  by  Government,  at 
the  expiration  of  which  they  are  obliged  to  look  out  for 
themselves.  The  captured  children  are  also  sent  to  the  vil- 
lages, where  they  are  kept  at  school  till  married,  which  is 
always  at  an  eariy  age.  At  the  head  of  each  village  is  a 
missionaiy,  who  receives  his  annual  support  from  the  Go- 
vernment, and  who  acts  in  the  double  capacity  of  minister 
and  schoolmaster.  v

laget  situated  to  the  westward  of  Sierra  Leone.  We  landed 
at  Kingstown,  the  former  residence  of  King  Tom.  The  house 
in  which  the  king  resided  is  in  ruins,  and  almost  hidden  from

The  British  ships  of  war  on  this  station  have  each  fron

The  other  articles  of  trade  are  ivory,  cam- wood,  wax*  and 
palm-oil.  We  sent  a  boat  from  Sierra  Leone  for  Mr.  Bacon, 
who  came  up  and  remained  with  us  two  days.  He  has  al- 
ready settled  himself  with  his  followers  (until  after  the  raint)

select  for  a  permanent  settlement. 

**  After  remaining  nine  days  at  Sierra  Leone,,  we  sailed

Spanish  papers,  that  it  is  impossible  to  condemn  them.  Two 
schooners,  the  Endymion  and  Esperanza,  we  sent  home.  We 
shall  leave  the  coast  in  the  course  of  three  or  four  days  for 
Port  Praya,  from  whence  we  shall  proceed  to  Teneriffe  for 
provisions. 

*^  The  Slave  Trade  is  carried  on  to  a  very  great  extent. , 
There  are  probably  not  less  than  300  vessels  on  the  coail 
engaged  in  that  traffic,  each  having  two  or  three  sets  ^ 
papers.  I  sincerely  hope  Government  have  revised  the  kcw, 
giving  us  more  authority.  You  have  no  idea  how  ctwStj 
these  poor  creatures  are  treated  by  the  monsters  engaged  te 
taking  them  from  the  coast.**

**  On  Wednesday  morning  I  went  with  some  people  to 
receive  them.  Those  who  remained  at  home  prepared  food 
for  their  poor  unfortunate  countrymen.  However,  we  were 
all  disappointed,  as  the  Court  of  Mixed  Commisnoo  head 
not  condemned  the  vessel. — Mr.  Reffell  (who  deserves  to  be 
noticed  for  his  humanity)  had  disembarked  the  Negroes^ 
and  no  doubt  saved  many  lives.  The  vessel  was  a  small 
schooner;  and  many  of  the  poor  creatures  were  ill  and 
reduced  to  skeletons.  As  the  Court  only  sat  on  Wednesday, 
I  sent  the  people  home  again,  and  staid  in  Freetown  myself 
to  wait  the  result. 

"On  Thursday  morning  I  was 'informed  that  the  Slaves 
and  vessel  were  condemned  by  the  Court.  The  description 
was  then  taken  ;  after  which  217  were  delivered  to  me : 
the  rest,  being  sick,  were  carried  to  Leicester  Mountain  to 
the  hospital. 

**  I  cannot  describe  the  scene  which  occurred  when  we 
arrived  at  Regent's  Town.  I  have  seen  many  Negroes 
landed,  but  never  beheld  such  an  aflPecting  sight.  As  soon 
as  we  came  in  sight  all  the  people  came  out  of  their  houses 
towards  the  road  to  meet  us,  with  the  greatest  acclamations. 
When  they  beheld  the  new  people  weak  and  faiut,  they 
carried  and  led  them  up  towards  my  house.  After  they  had 
laid  themselves  on  the  ground,  being  quite  exhausted,  many 
of  our  people  recognized  their  friends  and  relatives;  and 
there  was  a  general  cry  of  *  O,  master  I  my  sister !  my 
brother!  my  countryman !  he  lived  in  the  same  town!  my 
countrywoman  !  *  &c.  The  poor  creatures  being  faint,  just 
taken  out  of  the  hold  of  a  Slave-vessel,  and  unconscious  of 
what  had  befallen  them,  did  not  know  whether  they  should 
laugh  or  cry  when  they  beheld  the  countenances  of  those 
whom  they  had  supposed  long  dead,  but  now  saw  clothed 
and  clean,  and  perhaps  with  healthy  children  in  their  arms. 
In  short,  I  cannot  describe  the  scene :  it  was  too  affecting. 
No  one  could  refrain  from  shedding  tears  and  lifting  up  the

heart  in  pvayer  and  praise  to  the  wonder-working  God,  whose 
ways  are  in  tiie  deep. 

''The  school-boys  and  girls  brought  the  victaals  whiob 
they  had  prepared ;  and  all  the  people,  following  their  ex- 
ample, ran  to  their  houses  and  brought  what  they  had  got 
ready ;  and,  in  a  short  time,  their  unfortunate  countrymen 
were  overpowered  with  messes  of  every  description,  and  they 
made  a  good  dinner,  such  as  they  had  not  been  accustomed 
to  for  a  long  time.  Pine-apples,  ground-nuts,  and  oranges, 
were  also  brought  in  great  abundance. 

"  After  all  had  been  gratified,  it  getting  late,  I  begged

people  might  have  rest ;  which  being  done,  I  lodged  the  men 
and  boys  in  the  boys'  school,  and  the  women  and  girls  in  the 
girls*  school  The  two  permanent  school-houses  which  we 
have  built  I  now  find  of  great  service  ;  as  each  of  them  being 
73  feet  by  30,  and  having  two  floors,  will  contain  a  great 
number.''

''  Regent's  Town  now  wears  the  aspect  of  a  well  peopled 
village  in  our  happy  land ;  its  inhabitants  civilized,  indusr 
trioud,  honest,  and  neatly  clothed.  The  ground  allotted  .to 
each  fiimily  is  cultivated,  each  lot  being  distinctly  mar^d 
out.  I  have  frequently  ascended  an  eminence  near  the  tpwf 
to  behold  the  pleasing  scene  on  the  Sabbath-day — hundred^ 
pressmg  on  to  the  house  of  God,  at  the  sound  of  the  bell^ 
hungering  after  the  bread  of  life.  Nothing  but  sickness  pre^ 
vents  their  attendance  now.    What  a  lesson  does  this  teach

"  At  Bathurst,  a  captured  Negro,  converted  to  Christianity  by 
Mr.  Johnson's  ministry,  labours  among  the  people  with  much 
success.  He  has  been  propagating  the  Gospel  of  our  Lord 
Jesus  Christ  in  about  forty-seven  villages  on  the  coast :  he 
has  excited  the  attention  of  his  countrymen,  who  are  desirous 
to  hear  him  again.  He  is  a  bold  decided  champion  of  our 
Lord,  qualified  for  eminent  usefulness. 

*'  Before  I  conclude,  some  remarks  on  what  hsis  been  erro- 
neously asserted  of  the  African's  capacity,by  those  interested 
in  that  inhuman  traffic,  the  Slave  Trade,  may  not  be  unsea- 
sonable. By  them  it  has  been  asserted,  that  the  Africans  were 
bom  to  slavery;  that  thcirintellects  being  weak,  they  are  unable 
to  comprehend  the  sublime  truths  of  the  Christian  dispensa- 
tion ;  that  consequently  an  attempt  to  civilize  them  would  be 
vain.  Surely,  if  such  conclusions  can  be  drawn  from  their 
present  condition,  it  is  because  the  necessary  means  have 
been  withheld  from  them ;  their  capacities  have  never  been

cultivaiedy  the  sublime  truths  of  Christianity  never  preached: 
facts  now  prove  that  when  they  have  enjoyed  such  privileges,

receive  them.  Hundreds  now  in  the  mountains  of  Sierra 
Leone  have  become  monuments  of  that  Divine  grace  which 
knows  no  difference  between  Jew  or  Gentile,  bond  or  free, 
colour  or  clime* 

*'  Again;  the  Africans  are  very  tractable,  easily  persuaded 
by  those  who  manifest  a  concern  for>their  welfare :  strangers 
to  the  subtle  arguments  used  to  rob  the  Saviour  of  his

of  those  who  have  sent  them  the  bread  of  life. 

"  My  Christian  brethren,  through  whose  unwearied  exer-

your  hopes  are  realized  ;  and  while  you  have  cared  for  the , 
bodies  of  the  enslaved  Africans,  you  have  not  forgotten  their 
immortal  souk,  more  precious  than  ten  thousand  worlds.  It 
is  your  honour,  and  will,  I  am  assured,  tend  to  your  happi- 
ness, to  patronize  that  valuable  Society  which  sent  tlic 
Gospel  among  the  captured  Negroes.  You  have  now  their 
prayers  on  your  behalf,  and,  ere  long,  you  will  receive  your 
reward  in  that  world  of  joy  and  uninterrupted  felicity, 
where  you  will  shine  as  stars  in  the  firmament  of  heaven  : 
there  all  distinctions  ceas^  all  will  be  one  in  Christ  Jesus 
our  Lord.  What  we  now  see  is  only  the  first  fruits.  The 
Spirit  is  now  hovering  over  Africa,  waiting  to  breathe  on 
the  dry  bones.  Send  then  your  missionaries;  for  the  harvest 
truly  is  great,  but  the  labourers  arc  few."

tunity of  expressing  my  very  sincere  thanks  for  it ;  as  also  of 
testifying  to  you  all  the  interest  I  take  in  your  happy  re- 
establishment  in  the  government  of  Mauritius.

PROCLAMATION. 


^'  Inhabitants  of  Madagascar — 

**  You  are  none  of  you  ignorant  of  the  friendship  we  enjoy 
with  the  Governor  of  the  Mauritius,  and  the  devoted  at* 
tachment  we  have  avowed  to  bim :  his  attention,  unlike 
that  of  all  other  foreign  nations  that  have  visited  our 
shores,  has  been  directed  to  increase  our  happiness  and 
prosperity :  he  has  never  deprived  us  of  our  rights  or  our 
properties ;  he  has  not  sulffered  the  White  men  to  carry  off 
onr  children  into  slavery  ;  he  has  sent  us  people  to  teach  us 
arts  and  industry  unknown  before,  to  defend  us  against  our 
enemies,  and  to  prevent  famine  by  more  extensive  cultivation. 
We  are  happier  and  safer,  since  the  establishment  of  British 
dominion  in  our  neighbourhood ;  and  we  are  grateful  to  our 
good  father,  who  has  produced  for  us  these  blessings. 

**  His  nation  and  king  have  made  laws  to  prevent  you  from

joy  which  Radama  evinced  on  receiving  Mr.  Hastie ;  and 
he  most  cordially  greeted  me,  when  introduced  as  his  friend. 
Since  our  arrival,  the  acts  of  kindness  that  have  come  to 
my  knowledge  exceed  every  thing  that  I  could  expect;  and 
several  instances  prove  these  people  truly  grateful  for  past 
private  services  rendered  their  King,  who  proves  himself 
worthy  of  that  title,  as  his  sole  stody  is  the  instruction  of  his 
people,  and  the  W€^re  of  his  country. 

**  From  oircMnstances  observed  by  me  previously  to  arriv* 
ing  here,  I  must  say  I  am  truly  happy  at  the  fortunate  result 
of  your  Excellency's  endeavonrs  in  favour  of  a  people  who, 
I  deem,  by  your  meastor^s,  are  bow  secured  from  exportation 
to  a  strange  country ;  and  whose  talents  will,  when  brought 
forth,  shew  much  to  the  glory  of  the  British  Nation. 

**  The  anxiety  and  caution  of  the  King  is  the  strongest 
testimony  of  his  sincerity ;  and  his  measures  are  such  as 
must  ensure  happiness  to  hb  subjects,  and  prove  him  worthy 
of  your  regard.  I  must  therefore  express  a  wish,  that  the 
conclusion  will  meet  your  Excellency's  approbation,  as  on 
it  depends  the  salvation  of  millions,  and  will  prevent  the  ex- 
portation of  many  souls  that  would  be  hurried  into  Slavery, 
if  delay  was  admitted  of. 

'*  The  rcfasons  that  induce  me  to  remain  here  lire  many : 
I  find  myself  in  mnch  better  health  than  I  have  enjoyed  for 
some  time ;  I  find  the  climate  fine,  and  an  immense  opening 
for  doing  good ;  here  I  can  with  certainty  study  the  lan- 
guage, and  forward  the  great  work  devolving  upon  me ;  and, 
on  the  whole,  I  cotiiider  that  there  is  much  less  risk  in  re-

maining  here  than  undertaking  the  jonmey  down  and  fetum^

our  occasion  of  meeting  might  have  been  on  any  other  subject

unanimous  expression  of  the  public  voice  here,  in  reprobation 
of  that  traffic,  which  has  been  the  source  of  so  many 
troubles  to  the  colony.  I  trusted,  that  the  weight  and 
influence  of  the  real  landholders  and  proprietors,  and  true 
merchants,  would  have  sufficed  to  prevent  even  those  reptile 
vermin,  which  are  the  pest  of  all  societies,  from  attempting 
to  soil  our  shores  by  a  landing  on  our  coast.  I  hoped  that 
such  persons  would  have  been  obliged  to  fly  our  island,  if 
they  could  not  return  to  the  exercise  of  honest  industry. 

**  It  has  been,  however,  a  great  source  of  satisfaction  to 
me,  to  bear  testimony  to  the  purity  of  the  colony  from  this 


APPENDIX  DD,  383 

sin,  from  the  time  of  my  arrival  last  year,  until  the  present 
time.  This  solitary  exception  cannot  be  imputed  to  the 
colony  as  a  revival  of  such  a  traffic. 

*'  I  trust  that  the  result  of  this  day's  examination  will 
serve  as  a  lesson  to  all  Slave-traders,  if  such  should  still 
remain  within  our  island,  and  by  the  example  of  a  just 
severity,  and  the  public  sentiment,  declared  by  your  voice, 
conduce  more  to  the  prevention  of  such  crimes,  than  the 
strongest  means  that  could  otherwise  be  adopted. 

"  I  am  aware,  that  I  should  on  no  occasion  add  one  word 
that  might  give  rise  to  passion,  where  the  absence  of  all 
passion  is  necessary  for  the  calm  and  deliberate  decision  of 
justice  ;  for  I  am  convinced,  that  so  strongly  is  the  current  of 
public  feeling  and  opinion  now  against  the  Slave-traffickers 
in  this  colony,  that  the  duty  of  a  judge  should  rather  be

such  attempts  inspire  in  the  respectable  proprietors  of  this 
island  ;  but  I  am  confident  you  will,  on  the  present  occasion, 
acquit  yourselves  in  a  manner  equally  conducive  to  the  ends 
of  justice,  honourable  to  yourselves,  and  satisfactory  to  the 
colony,  who  look  to  the  decision  of  this  day,  as  of  the  very 
highest  importance  to  the  public, — as  assuring  their  lasting 
tranquillity,  and  tending  to  enable  the  Government  to  turn 
its  sole  and  undivided  attention  to  the  revival  and  extension 
of  our  commerce,  and  the  improvement  of  our  agriculture. 

**  Until  thb  desirable  end,  however,  of  a  total  extirpation 
of  the  Slave  Traffic,  is  irrevocably  secured,  it  behoves  me,  as 
governor,  responsible  for  such  atrocities  not  being  passed 
unpunished,  to  use  every  means  which  are  confided  to  me 
by  my  sovereign  and  by  the  laws,  to  effect  its  final  annihila- 
tion ;  and  I  pledge  myself,  that  as  none  of  these  means  have 
ever  yet  been  left  idle  in  my  hands,  none  shall  henceforth  be 
neglected,  to  pursue  to  the  utmost  all  criminals  engaged  in 
such  a  course.  If  they  escape  at  one  moment  the  reach  of 
the  law,  it  will  be  but  for  a  time,  for  the  vigilance  of  the 
Government,  and  of  the  officers  of  justice,  shall  never  sleep 
till  they  are  seized  and  brought  before  this  Court.

HH. 

Copy  of  the  Address  circulated,  prior  to  the  Annual 
General  Meeting  of  the  Institution^  to  the  Friends 
of  Africa. 

*'  FiFTBEN  years  have  elapsed  since  Great  Britain,  by  an 
Act  of  the  Legislature,  prohibited  its  subjects,  under  heavy 
penalties,  from  taking  any  part  in  that  trade  which  has 
since  been  described,  by  the  unanimous  voice  of  the  great 
Powers  of  Europe,  assembled  in  Congress  at  Vienna,  as  *  a 
scourge  which  has  long  desolated  Africa,  degraded  Eun^, 
and  afflicted  humanity  ;'  and  it  is  now  classed  by  the  British 
Pariiament  amongst  the   foulest  crimes.     Soon  after  the 


APPENDIX  HH.  S95 

pasBiDg  of  that  Act,  a  considerable  number  of  those  who 
had  strenaously  exerted  themselves,  through  a  long  series 
of  years,  to  expose  the  enormities  inseparable  from  this 
horrid  traffic,  and  to  procure  the  co-operation  of  the  Friends 
of  Humanity  in  its  Abolition,  formed  themselves  into  a 
Society,  under  the  name  of  '  The  African  Institution,'  with 
a  view,  not  only  to  promote  the  civilization  of  much-injured 
Africa,  but  abo,  as  essential  to  this  object,  to  watch  most 
carefully  over  the  conduct  of  those  who  might  attempt  to 
evade  the  Abolition  Laws. 

*'  Great  Britain  had  the  less  difficulty  in  etfecting  the 
Abolition  of  this  traffic,  by  reason  of  the  liberty  of  her 
Press,  and  the  nature  of  her  Government,  which  rendered  it 
comparatively  easy  to  convey  the  necessary  information 
respecting  the  real  character  of  this  trade  to  all  classes  of 
Society.  But  the  case  is  very  different  in  many  of  the 
nations  of  the  continent.  In  few,  perhaps  in  none  of  them, 
do  the  same  fiEkcilities  to  the  diffusion  of  knowledge  and  the 
forming  of  Societies  for  the  objects  of  benevolence  exist ; 
and  consequently  very  erroneous  ideas  prevail  abroad  on  the 
subject  of  the  African  Slave-trade. 

"  The  information  redeived  from  time  to  time  by  The 
African  Institution— of  the  horrid  crimes  perpetrated  in 
Africa,  and  on  the  high  seas,  by  miscreants  who  make  it 
their  business  to  buy  and  sell  their  fellow-creatures,  and  of 
the  alarming  increase  of  this  abominable  traffic  under  the 
flags  «f  France,  Spain,  Portugal,  and  the  Netherlands— is  of 
sttch  a  nature,  as  to  render  it  the  duty  of  the  Institution  to 
give  the  utmost  publicity  to  the  fiatcts  which  are  constantly 
commg  to  their  knowledge,  and  to  call  the  attention  of  the 
British  Nation,  in  a  very  particular  manner,  to  the  enormi- 
ties now  practised  upon  the  persons  of  the  helpless  children 
of  Africa ;  enormities  never  exceeded  in  the  annab  of  op- 
pression and  cruelty.  At  the  present  moment  vast  numbers 
of  innocent  men,  women,  and  children,  are  languishing  in  the 
hands  of  their  tormentors ;  many  are  suffering  a  most  cruel 
and  lingering  death  by  suffocation  in  the  holds  of  Slave- 
ships  ;  thousands  are  on  their  way  to  interminable  slavery. 


396  APPENDIX  HH. 

to  which  they  will  iniaUibly  be  coasigqed^  unlets  prevkmsly 
released  by  death,  or  rescued  by  tbe  iBterre&tioD  of  some 
ttierciful  hand,  from  those  dealers  in  huaian  blood,  whom 
the  American  Government  has  declared  to  be  pirates,  and 
who,  instead  of  being  protected  and  sheltered,  ought  to  be 
branded  by  every  civilised  State  as  enemies  to  the  human 
race. 

**  The  African  Institution  is  persuaded,  thai  in  France,  now 
most  deeply  implicated  in  this  cruel  traffic,  as  well  as  in  the 
Netherlands,  Portugal,  and  Spain,  the  public  at  large  are 
not  yet  informed  of  the  real  nature  and  vast  extent  of  the 
crimes  daily  and  hourly  perpetrated  by  the  subjects  of  diehr 
respective  countries,  who  are  engaged  in  the  African  Slave* 
trade.  The  Directors  have  therefore  determined,  if  fnrnisk^ 
ed  with  the  means,  to  publish  in  various  languages  the  &cti 
which  are  ahnost  daily  communicated  to  them,  in  the  firm 
conviction  that,  when  these  fiMsls  shall  be  generally  known^ 
the  wile  and  the  good  of  all  nations  wiH  rise  up,  and,  wHh 
the  voice  as  of  one  man,  solicit  their  respective  Oovemmeatn 
to  abolish  a  traffic  marited  in  every  stage  wiUi  blood,  db« 
graceful  to  every  nation  that  does  not  use  the  greatest  cker^ 
tions  kit  its  utter  extbction,  and  a  standing  reproach  to  the 
Christian  name.  ' 

**  The  African  Institution,  therefore,  invites  the  Friends  of 
Humanity  and  Rdigion  to  its  Sixteenth  Anniversary  Meetmg,
